It stays silent on bare prepositional 'as' ('as a rule', 'as the manager asked', 'as the author of this work'), on the definite article in the same slot ('Take the photo'), and on the same closed-class words inside specific third-person narration ('He took a seat', 'I saw a photo').

Last spring the regional agricultural board commissioned an independent survey of the orchards along the northern ridge. The team arrived in early April, after the last frost, and spent three weeks walking the rows with clipboards and handheld sensors. Each block was sampled twice, once at dawn and once in the late afternoon, so that the readings could be compared across the day.

The orchardists were cooperative but skeptical. Several of them had already lost a third of their trees to a fungus that spread through the root systems after the wet winter, and they wanted to know whether the remaining stock could be saved. The survey team measured soil moisture, leaf colour and the density of the canopy, then sent the samples to a laboratory in the capital.

Nothing about the results was straightforward. The laboratory reported that nitrogen levels in the eastern blocks were normal, while the western blocks showed a pattern the technicians had not seen before. A second round of tests was ordered, and the board asked for a preliminary summary before the summer recess.

The summary arrived in June. It said the damage was uneven, that some farms would recover within a season and that others would need to replant entirely. The board met on a Thursday and argued for most of the afternoon. In the end it agreed to fund a replanting programme for the worst affected farms and to extend the survey for another year so that the pattern could be tracked as it developed.

By then the board had spent most of its reserve. The chair reminded the members that the survey had been their idea, that the laboratory bills were already paid and that the farms could not wait another year for a decision. The members listened, argued briefly and then voted without much debate.

By the autumn the picture had changed again. The eastern blocks, which had looked healthy in April, began to lose leaves ahead of schedule, and the technicians who returned to the ridge found the same fungus in two of them. The board's chair called the findings disappointing but not unexpected, and said the programme would continue regardless of the cost.

The board also commissioned a map of the affected blocks, and the map showed the same pattern the technicians had seen in the spring.

When the full report was finally published, the headline figure was worse than anyone had feared. Across the region the harvest had fallen by as much as 40 percent.
